en: The Sūtra on the Adornment of the Light of Wisdom that Transcends the Realms of All Buddhas;
the translator’s name lost, appended to the Qin Records.
Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was dwelling in the Bodhi-light Dharma Forest in the kingdom of Magadha.
The palace was radiant, constructed through great merit, capable of inspiring immense joy in all who beheld it.
Upon a high lion throne adorned with lotus flowers of immeasurable virtue sat the Buddha— his mind pure as the Perfectly All-Knowing One,
practicing peerless right conduct, having reached the state of the equal Dharma of all Buddhas with a mind free from obstruction.
Having reached the stage of non-retrogression, they do not abandon the boundless buddha-activities;
they dwell securely in the inconceivable, incline toward the signless dharma, and realize the equality of the three periods of time.

Their bodies fill the worlds, they know all dharmas without doubt, and their bodies of omniscience possess immeasurable wisdom. They are upheld by the great bodhisattvas and have already reached all...

The Buddha’s peerless dhyāna is ultimately fulfilled; having attained the wisdom of liberation, he turns the wheel of Dharma with great kindness and great compassion, possessing an ultimately boundless form-body.
And there was an assembly of sixty-two thousand other bhikṣus,
whose names were: Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Aniruddha, Subhūti, Kātyāyana, Mahākapphiṇa, Revata, and Nanda.
...Nadī-Kāśyapa, Gayā-Kāśyapa, Panthaka-Maitrāyaṇīputra,
Gavāmpati, Cūḍapanthaka, Dravyamālika, Kātyāyanīputra, Cunda, Mahākauṣṭhila, Rāhula, Ānanda, and so forth.
This assembly of sixty-two thousand— whose every concentration and every practice is complete,
who have equally entered the nature of all phenomena, who dwell nowhere and rely on nothing, who have transcended all afflictions, who have entered the Buddha-realm,
who follow a single Dharma toward omniscience, who do not abandon the path to omniscience, and who delight in omniscience without regressing— [all gathered together].
She had already reached the foremost perfection of vipaśyanā and had given rise to the spheres of practice of all skillful means,
together with ten thousand bhikṣuṇīs.

The bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī and the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā—equally entered into the pure dharmas of all benevolent deities; they drew near to all-knowledge and entered the illumination of all-knowledge. They were skillfully proficient in the naturelessness of all dharmas, entering the naturelessness of all dharmas, entering the signlessness of all dharmas, and attaining the reality-limit of all dharmas. Knowing that all dharmas are unarisen, they dwelt securely in the inconceivable samādhi of liberation, teaching and transforming sentient beings without deliberate effort or conceptualization, yet able to manifest the four types of dignified deportment.
Furthermore, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas equal in number to the atoms within unspeakably many billions of nayutas of ten buddha-worlds,
whose names were: the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, Universal Eye Bodhisattva, Universal Transformation Bodhisattva,
Universal Wisdom Bodhisattva, Universal Flame Bodhisattva, Universal Radiance Bodhisattva, Universal Clarity Bodhisattva, and Universal Light Bodhisattva.
Bodhisattva Vidyutprabha, Bodhisattva Samantaketu, Bodhisattva Samantamati,
Bodhisattva Mahāvikrama, Bodhisattva Mahādharavikrama, Bodhisattva Mahāṛddhi, Bodhisattva Mahāṛddhirāja,
Bodhisattva Mahāvikrama, Bodhisattva Mahāvikramabala, Bodhisattva Mahāvinardita, and Bodhisattva Mahā...
The Bodhisattva Bimbasārabala, the Bodhisattva Mahāgandhahastin, the Bodhisattva Mahācandra, the Bodhisattva Sucandra,
the Bodhisattva Samantaprabhācandra, the Bodhisattva Dharmavimalacandra, the Bodhisattva Arciścandra, the Bodhisattva Candraprabha,
the Bodhisattva Prabhāsamuñcanacandra, the Bodhisattva Pūrṇacandra, and the Bodhisattva Brahmamahā...
The Bodhisattva Sovereign; the Bodhisattva Resounding Voice of Brahmā and Śakra; the Bodhisattva Earth-Rumbling Sound; the Bodhisattva Resonance of the Dharma Realm;
the Bodhisattva Eliminating All Māra-Realm Sounds; the Bodhisattva Resonance of the Dharma Drum;
the Bodhisattva Universal Speech Sound; the Bodhisattva Non-Conceptual Sound; and the Bodhisattva Ground-Level Resonance.
The Bodhisattvas: Sarvasvaradhātugaganasvara Bodhisattva, Samantottara Bodhisattva, Samantavimalottara Bodhisattva, Guṇakośa Bodhisattva, Prabhāsa Bodhisattva, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva,
Ratnakośa Bodhisattva, Candrakośa Bodhisattva, Sūryakośa Bodhisattva, and Taptaraśmikośa Bodhisattva.
...Sāgaramati, Padmaśrīgarbha Bodhisattva, Matisattva, Mahāmatisattva, Jayamati Bodhisattva, Vighuṣṭamati Bodhisattva,
Vipulamati Bodhisattva, Uttaramati Bodhisattva, Vardhamānamati Bodhisattva, Anantamati Bodhisattva, Vyūhamati Bodhisattva, Bodhimati Bodhisattva, and An...
The Bodhisattva Kṣepāśaya, the Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, the Bodhisattva Merupradīpa, the Bodhisattva Mahāpradīpa,
the Bodhisattva Dharmolkāpradīpa, the Bodhisattva Sarvāvabhāsapradīpa, the Bodhisattva Samantaprabhāsa,
the Bodhisattva Sarvatamo’ndhakāravidhamanapradīpa, the Bodhisattva Sarvagatipratibhāsaprada, and the Bodhisattva Ekaraśmi.
Dīpa Bodhisattva, Candradīpa Bodhisattva, Sūryadīpa Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta Bodhisattva,
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Mahāvīryapāpta Bodhisattva, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva,
Guhyaguhya Bodhisattva, Apāyajah Bodhisattva, and Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva.

Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, Bodhisattva Maitreyaghoṣa, Bodhisattva Padmapāṇi, Bodhisattva Sūryaprabha, Bodhisattva Vīramatiraṇu, Bodhisattva Vajramati, Bodhisattva Sarvadhātupramardaka, Bodhisattva Māraparājita, and Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin.

The Bodhisattva Illumined by a Hundred Lights, the Bodhisattva Unconquerable by Great Māras, the Bodhisattva Unarisen, the Bodhisattva Invincible, the Bodhisattva Inaccessible, the Bodhisattva of Inapproachable Resolve, the Bodhisattva Sweeping Away Evil Destinies, and the Bodhisattva Maitreya.
Such bodhisattvas as these— bodhisattva-mahāsattvas equal in number to the atoms of ten unspeakable trillions of nayutas of buddha-worlds—
having gathered from other worlds through the succession of a single birth, they thoroughly understand sentient beings, bring them to maturity,
abide securely in the wisdom and skillful means of bodhisattvas, and enter into worldly dharmas.
Having realized the state of *nirvāṇa* and observed that all habitual calculations have been fully understood,
they practice the abandonment of activity while taking up the vow to gather in sentient beings through unceasing clarity; they skillfully enter into the infinite and the non-central,
clearly understanding the karmic fruits of all sentient beings without fail, and through the wisdom of non-attainment, they observe the fetters and afflictions of sentient beings.

Possessing skillful means and wisdom, they thoroughly understand the meanings and phrases of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present; they are well able to receive and uphold them, discerning them with wisdom.
Entering into both the mundane and supramundane realms—which are neither boundless nor have a center—they are able to contemplate conditioned and unconditioned phenomena.
Facing the wisdom of all Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present, they realize the mind moment by moment.
Those births and deaths— initial birth, renunciation of the world, ascetic practices, sitting at the Bodhi tree,
subduing Māra and attaining Buddhahood, turning the wheel of Dharma, and entering parinirvāṇa— are all performed without departing from sentient beings as he gives rise to the karma of bodhicitta.

These bodhisattvas, by means of the mental object of a single sentient being’s mind, enter into the mental objects of the minds of all sentient beings; they give rise to the ground of wisdom through skillful means, do not regress from the bodhisattva body, and attain the ground of omniscience. They practice without falling back, never severing the conduct of a bodhisattva, and enter into effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*).

For the sake of a single sentient being, they perform boundless deeds while remaining in non-action; they turn the wheel of Dharma to transform and teach the world, clearly understanding and upholding the root of all Buddha-dharmas, thereby succeeding to the lineage of the Tathāgatas so that it shall never be severed.

In worlds where no Buddha dwells, they are able to manifest as Buddhas; they are able to purify defiled and evil worlds; they are able to eliminate all karmic obstacles of bodhisattvas, causing them to enter into correspondence with the dharma of non-obstruction, correspondence with all worlds equal to space, and correspondence with the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) that is non-obstructive; they know all retributions produced by karma as being equal to the *dharmadhātu*, corresponding to the retributions produced according to those causes and conditions, and they seal all dharmas with that seal.

Corresponding with the knowledge of equality (*samatājñāna*), they manifest all images; corresponding with the knowledge of equality, they understand all conventional designations within echoing sounds.

These bodhisattvas abide in the inconceivable samādhi of liberation, sport in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, and dwell securely in the infinite bodies of the Buddhas. Possessing all dhāraṇīs, they manifest all worlds from a single pore, accomplishing the pure abodes of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present. They uphold supreme vows and practices, perfect the conduct of Samantabhadra, and fully comprehend the initial birth and parinirvāṇa of all Buddhas, entreating them to preach the Dharma for the benefit and peace of sentient beings.

Within a single pore, he manifests throughout the ten directions his initial birth, renunciation of the world, the practice of asceticism through skillful means, sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, subduing Māra and attaining Buddhahood, turning the wheel of Dharma, and entering parinirvāṇa.
These bodhisattvas, through their correspondence with wisdom, are able from a single seat to shake all worlds in the ten directions;
within a single buddha-field, they can universally adorn all buddha-worlds;
having thoroughly understood the adornment of one buddha-world, they can manifest all buddha-worlds.
Within the assemblies of all Tathāgatas throughout the worlds of the ten directions, they are able to manifest the assembly of a single Tathāgata;
within the assembly of a single Tathāgata, they are able to manifest the assemblies of all Tathāgatas throughout the ten directions;
they clearly understand that the preaching of the Dharma has neither center nor periphery.
They are able to manifest all sentient beings within their own bodies;
they can manifest many Buddhas within a single Buddha-body, and manifest a single Buddha within many Buddha-bodies;
they can cause their own bodies to appear throughout the worlds of the ten directions, and having mastered the three periods of time, they can manifest the body of a single sentient being.

They manifest the future world within the past world, and the past world within the future world; they manifest the present world within the past world, and the past world within the present world; they manifest the present world within the future world, and the future world within the present world.

They are able to enter and emerge from immeasurable and innumerable dhyānas and samāpattis with a single body, and to enter and emerge from a single dhyāna and samāpatti with immeasurable and innumerable bodies.

They are able to manifest enlightenment in all bodies; they can manifest all sentient beings within the body of a single sentient being, and manifest a single sentient being within the bodies of all sentient beings.
One can manifest all sentient beings within a single Buddha-body, and manifest a single Buddha within the bodies of all sentient beings;
one can manifest all bodies— the Dharma-body and the bodies of sentient beings— and within all worlds, one can manifest a single world,
distribute a single world to manifest as many worlds, and cause the worlds of the ten directions to...
Entering a single pore, one can manifest all sentient beings and the places where all Buddhas attain enlightenment through the power of their vows;
one can manifest the maturation of sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions and the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
one can manifest the cultivation of bodhisattva practices within a single world throughout incalculable eons; and one can manifest a single mind.
Born in all worlds throughout the ten directions, among all sentient beings in every world—whether born from a womb, an egg, moisture, or by transformation;
whether possessing form or formless, with perception or without perception;
having two feet, four feet, no feet, or many feet; gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and so forth—
Gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā,
the Four Heavenly Kings, humans, and non-humans— according to what has been matured in them, he teaches and transforms sentient beings with effortlessness,
and does not give rise to formal conduct through deliberate thought.

Within a single atom, they can manifest all sentient beings of immeasurable, innumerable, and ineffable worlds, yet there is no crowding; they can manifest the deeds, postures, and karmic rewards of immeasurable, innumerable, and ineffable eons within a single thought-moment, and manifest such activities throughout immeasurable, innumerable, and ineffable eons. Their minds are effortless and free from deliberation as they manifest their physical forms, postures, and various transformations.
Furthermore, there were other bodhisattvas who possessed immeasurable hundreds of millions of nayutas of meritorious virtues.

There were also unspeakable numbers of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, the four heavenly kings, humans, non-humans, and others, who had come from various buddha-worlds to assemble here.

From this world, hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Cāturmahārājakāyika devas—each Cāturmahārājakāyika deva accompanied by one great deva and their various retinues—came to the place where the Buddha was, prostrating, making offerings, and listening to the true Dharma.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Śakras, lords of the gods; immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kings of the Yāma heaven; immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kings of the Tuṣita heaven; immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kings of the Nirmāṇarati heaven; and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kings of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven, who came to where the Buddha was to pay homage, make offerings, and listen to the True Dharma.

Furthermore, various celestial beings and their retinues also came to the Buddha’s presence to pay homage, make offerings, and listen to the True Dharma. There were also immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Brahmā kings;

immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Mahābrahmā kings; immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Parīttābha devas; immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Apramāṇābha devas; immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Ābhāsvara devas; immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Parīttaśubha devas; immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Apramāṇaśubha devas; and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Śubhakṛtsna devas, up to and including all the devas of the Akaniṣṭha heaven. Each of these hosts of devas came together to the Buddha’s presence to pay homage, make offerings, and listen to the True Dharma.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of devas from the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, as well as the son of Mahesvara, who came to where the Buddha was, prostrating, making offerings, and listening to the true Dharma.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nāga kings; immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of yakṣa kings; immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of gandharva kings; immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kiṃnara kings; and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of mahoraga kings, who came to where the Buddha was, prostrated, made offerings, and listened to the true Dharma.
Furthermore, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* numbers of humans and non-humans came to where the Buddha was, prostrating, making offerings, and listening to the True Dharma.
Additionally, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of *upāsakas* and *upāsikās* came to where the Buddha was, prostrating, making offerings, and listening to the True Dharma.

Furthermore, there were mountain deities, tree deities, and deities of grasses and trees, as well as the deities of Mount Meru, Mahāmeru, Mucilinda, Mahāmucilinda, the Snowy Mountains, and the Iron Ring Mountains, who came to where the Buddha was, prostrated, made offerings, and listened to the True Dharma.

Furthermore, there were deities of small seas, great seas, small rivers, great rivers, lakes, ponds, and so forth, who came to where the Buddha was, prostrated, made offerings, and listened to and received the True Dharma.
Furthermore, there were deities of villages, towns, kingdoms, and cities who came to where the Buddha was, prostrating, making offerings, and listening to the True Dharma.

Additionally, there were deities dwelling in the abodes of nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas who came to where the Buddha was, prostrating, making offerings, and listening to the True Dharma; through the Buddha’s supernatural power, none of them experienced any crowding or distress.

Furthermore, there were hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Moon Devas, and likewise hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Sun Devas; each of these devas, leading their vast retinues, came to where the Buddha was, prostrating, making offerings, and listening to the true Dharma.
Furthermore, the great nāga king Anavatapta came to where the Buddha was, prostrated, made offerings, and listened to the true Dharma.

At that time, the World-Honored One’s radiance shone forth, surpassing the entire assembly; it was like the full moon on the fifteenth day—perfect, bright, and pure, free from all clouds and shadows—its brilliance outshining all the stars.
Thus the World-Honored One’s radiance shone forth, surpassing all the devas of Śakra and Brahmā; the Buddha’s body remained as immovable as Sumeru, the King of Mountains.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin, saying:
“O Son of the Buddha!
"This body of the Tathāgata abides immovably.
Having spoken thus, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Subduer of All Obstructions addressed Mañjuśrī again, saying:

“In this assembly, some see the Buddha wishing to leave home and cross the city walls; some see him having already left home; some see him practicing asceticism; some see him proceeding toward the Bodhi tree; some see him already seated at the tree of enlightenment; some see him surrounded by immeasurable and innumerable Māras; some see him having already defeated the armies of Māra; and some see immeasurable and innumerable devas, nāga kings, yakṣas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, Śakras, and Brahmās saying these words:
‘May the Tathāgata be victorious!’”
Some see the Buddha being invited by Śakra; some see the Buddha being invited by Brahmā; and some see the Buddha being invited by the Four Heavenly Kings.
"Furthermore, among those in this assembly, some see the Buddha preaching the Dharma of generosity for my sake;
some see him preaching the Dharma of ethical discipline for my sake; some see him preaching the Dharma of patience for my sake;
some see him preaching the Dharma of diligence for my sake; some see him preaching the Dharma of meditative concentration for my sake; and some see him [preaching] for my sake..."
I preach the Dharma of wisdom; for some, seeing them as such, I preach the Dharma of skillful means; for some, seeing them as such, I preach the Dharma of aspiration;
for some, seeing them as such, I preach the Dharma of the Śrāvakas; for some, seeing them as such, I preach the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas;
for some, seeing them as such, I preach the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas; and for some, seeing them as such, I preach the Dharma of birth in the hells.
Some saw me teaching the dharma for birth as a hungry ghost; some saw me teaching the dharma for birth as an animal;
some saw me teaching the dharma for birth as a human; some saw me teaching the dharma for birth among the Four Great Kings;
some saw me teaching the dharma for birth among the Thirty-three Gods; and some saw me teaching the dharma for birth in the Yāma Heaven.
Regarding the dharma of birth: some see me as teaching the dharma of birth in Tuṣita Heaven;
some see me as teaching the dharma of birth in Nirmāṇarati Heaven; some see me as teaching the dharma of birth in Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven;
some see me as teaching the dharma of birth in the Brahma Heavens; and some see me as teaching the dharma of birth as a Cakravartin King.

Furthermore, among those in this assembly, some may see the Tathāgata’s body as being two *vyāma* in height; some may see the Buddha’s body as being one *krośa* in height; some may see the Buddha’s body as being two *krośa* in height; some may see the Buddha’s body as being one *yojana* in height; some may see the Buddha’s body as being ten *yojana* in height; some may see the Buddha’s body as being a thousand *yojana* in height; some may see the Buddha’s body as being ten, twenty, thirty, forty, or fifty thousand *yojana* in height; some may see the Buddha’s body as being a hundred thousand *yojana* in height; some may see the Buddha’s body as being ten, twenty, thirty, forty, or fifty hundred thousand *yojana* in height; some may see the Buddha’s body as being eighty-four thousand *yojana* in height; or some may see the Buddha’s body as exceeding hundreds of thousands of *yojana* beyond measure.
“Some see the Buddha’s body as the color of purple-gold; some see the Buddha’s body as the color of precious lapis lazuli;
some see the Buddha’s body as the color of Indra-blue maṇi jewels; some see the Buddha’s body as the color of great blue maṇi jewels;
some see the Buddha’s body as the color of fire-light maṇi jewels; or they see the Buddha’s body...”
The color of the maṇi-jewel lotus; or seeing the Buddha’s body as having a color surpassing that of the Śakra-maṇi jewel;
or seeing the Buddha’s body as having the color of the vajra-light maṇi-jewel; or seeing the Buddha’s body as having the color of the maṇi-jewel light of all celestial jewels;
or seeing the Buddha’s body as having the color of the maṇi-jewel light of the sun and moon; or...
They see the Buddha’s body as the color of crystal-maṇi jewels; or they see the Buddha’s body as the color of the maṇi jewels of the Sovereign Heavenly King;
or they see the Buddha’s body as the color of the maṇi jewels that are a mass of all radiance;
or they see the Buddha’s body as the color of the maṇi jewels with lion-manes; or they see the Buddha’s body as the color of the maṇi jewels of the lion-banner.
Regarding form, some see the Buddha-body as having the color of a sea of pure, adorned, and all-pervading light mani-jewels;
others see the Buddha-body as having the color of wish-fulfilling mani-jewels.

“Mañjuśrī! These sentient beings, seeing the body of the Tathāgata, hearing the Dharma he preaches, entering the conduct of the Tathāgata, and reaching the realm of the Buddha—each of those sentient beings perceives the Tathāgata according to their own practice.”

“Mañjuśrī! In the eastern direction, there are worlds beyond measure, inconceivable, and ineffable, filled with devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakras, Brahmās, the Four Great Kings, humans, non-humans, and so forth.

As it is in the eastern direction, so it is in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir—beyond measure, inconceivable, and ineffable, filled with devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakras, Brahmās, the Four Great Kings, humans, non-humans, and so forth; the great assembly fills [them] completely, like a grove of bamboo, like a field of sugarcane, or like a field of rice or hemp.”
"Mañjuśrī! If sentient beings are able to see the Tathāgata, those sentient beings can then be transformed; they shall stand one fathom away from the Tathāgata and gaze up at him."
At that time, sentient beings, according to their perceptions, see the Tathāgata manifesting the four modes of deportment before each of them. Mañjuśrī!
If he brings sentient beings to maturity by means of preaching the Dharma, all those sentient beings hear that preaching of the Dharma.
Mañjuśrī! If one matures sentient beings through conduct, those sentient beings see only the conduct of the Buddha. Mañjuśrī!

That which is manifested by the Tathāgata involves no difference in function and no difference in thought; yet, according to the natures of sentient beings, what they perceive differs from one another. Mañjuśrī!

Just as on the night of the fifteenth day, the people of Jambudvīpa each see the moon appearing above them, yet the moon does not form the thought, "I am appearing above them," nor does it form the thought to cause them to see it.
Why is this? Because it is the unshared dharma. Mañjuśrī!

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, appears before every sentient being within the great assembly, such that each perceives him as being right in front of themselves. Yet the Buddha does not form the thought, "I shall manifest before them," nor does he form the thought, "I shall cause them to see me. Those who are ready to be transformed perceive him according to their own individual vision.
Why is this? Because they are the unshared dharmas. "Mañjuśrī!

It is like a most excellent crystal maṇi jewel that assumes various colors according to the various garments [upon which it rests]: if the jewel is placed upon a yellow garment, the jewel becomes yellow;
if placed upon a red garment, the jewel becomes red;
if placed upon a blue garment, the jewel becomes blue.
This maṇi jewel does not intentionally or deliberately cause itself to become a different color;
likewise, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, manifests various colors by means of sentient beings.
If there are sentient beings who should be transformed by seeing a golden color, they see the Tathāgata’s body as golden in color;
if they should be transformed by seeing the color of crystal maṇi jewels, they see the Tathāgata as the color of crystal maṇi jewels;
if they should be transformed by seeing the color of pearls, they see the Tathāgata as the color of pearls.
To those who should be transformed by seeing the color of the Indra-maṇi jewel, they see the Tathāgata as having the color of the Indra-maṇi jewel;
to those who should be transformed by seeing the color of the great blue maṇi jewel, they see the Tathāgata as having the color of the great blue maṇi jewel;
to those who should be transformed by seeing the color of the maṇi jewel that is a mass of all radiances, they see the Tathāgata as having the color of the maṇi jewel that is a mass of all radiances.
To those who should be transformed by seeing the color of the lion-maned maṇi jewel, they see the Tathāgata in the color of the lion-maned maṇi jewel;
to those who should be transformed by seeing the color of the maṇi jewel atop the lion-banner, they see the Tathāgata in the color of the maṇi jewel atop the lion-banner;

to those who should be transformed by seeing the color of the ocean-abiding pure-ornament universal-light maṇi jewel, they see the Tathāgata in the color of the ocean-abiding pure-ornament universal-light maṇi jewel.
To those who should be transformed by seeing the color of the lightning-lamp mani-jewel, they see the Tathāgata as having the color of the lightning-lamp mani-jewel;
to those who should be transformed by seeing the color of the water-purifying mani-jewel, they see the Tathāgata as having the color of the water-purifying mani-jewel.

Mañjuśrī! If there are sentient beings who should see the Tathāgata and are to be transformed by the appearance of Śakra, Brahmā, or the Four Great Kings, they shall see the Tathāgata in the form of Śakra, Brahmā, or the Four Great Kings.

Thus, from the hells, animals, hungry ghosts, and King Yama, up to the formless realm—including those born from wombs, eggs, moisture, or transformation; those with form or without form; those with perception or without perception—whosoever undergoes transformation according to their physical characteristics, all those sentient beings perceive the Tathāgata as possessing various marks.
The Tathāgata likewise does not engage in intentional discrimination, thinking: "Let this sentient being who wishes to see me in a golden color not see me in the color of crystal-maṇi;
let this sentient being who wishes to see me in the color of crystal-maṇi not see me in a golden color;
let this sentient being who wishes to see me in the color of crystal-maṇi not see me in the color of pearl."
If these sentient beings wish to see my pearl-like color, do not let them see my crystal-maṇi color;
if these sentient beings wish to see my indra-nīla maṇi color, do not let them see my great blue maṇi color;
if these sentient beings wish to see my great blue maṇi color, do not let them see my indra-nīla maṇi color.
For those beings who wish to see my color of the *sarvālokasamuccaya-maṇi* jewel, do not let them see my color of the *siṃhakeśara-maṇi* jewel;
for those beings who wish to see my color of the *siṃhakeśara-maṇi* jewel, do not let them see my color of the *sarvālokasamuccaya-maṇi* jewel;
for those beings who wish to see my color of the *siṃhadhvaja-agra-maṇi* jewel, do not let them see my color of the *sāgarastha-viśuddhavyūha-samantaprabha-maṇi* jewel.
For those beings who wish to see my ocean-abiding pure adornment of universal radiance mani-jewel color, let them not see my lion-banner mani-jewel color;
for those beings who wish to see my lightning-lamp mani-jewel color, let them not see my water-purity mani-jewel color;
for those beings who wish to see my water-purity mani-jewel color, let them not see my lightning-flame mani-jewel color.
If these sentient beings wish to see my form as Śakra, Brahmā, or the Four Heavenly Kings, let them not see my form as one in the hells, among animals, as a hungry ghost, or as Yama;
if these sentient beings wish to see my form as one in the hells, among animals, as a hungry ghost, or as Yama, let them not see my form as Śakra, Brahmā, or the Four Heavenly Kings.
The Tathāgata does not engage in volitional thought; without effort and without discrimination, he accomplishes his work. “Mañjuśrī!
Just as in the place where the sovereign maṇi-jewel originates, iron cannot arise, nor can any other implements be produced there.”
The sovereign king maṇi-jewel also does not form a mental intention, thinking, "In this place, iron and various implements should not arise. Mañjuśrī!
Where the sovereign king maṇi-jewel arises spontaneously, there iron never arises, nor can any other implements ever arise.

Mañjuśrī! In such a realm of the Buddha, the place where the Tathāgata is born, even the Nirgrantha non-Buddhists cannot arise; various false views cannot arise; all forms of distraction do not arise; the five heinous crimes do not arise; the ten unwholesome paths do not arise; the laws of restraint do not arise; the light of the sun and moon does not arise; the lights of Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, and other devas do not arise; the light of various precious maṇi jewels does not arise; the light of fire does not arise; the light of lightning does not arise; nor do the reckonings of a single thought-moment or half a thought-moment, of a month or half a month, or of a year or half a year arise.
“Mañjuśrī! Although the Tathāgata brings sentient beings to maturity, he does not engage in deliberation; his mind is free from effort, yet everything is accomplished.”

Mañjuśrī! Just as when a person is touched by the light of a great sapphire mani jewel, that person immediately takes on the color of the great sapphire mani jewel, yet the great sapphire mani jewel does not form any intentional thought.

If a person is touched by the light of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, that person immediately becomes the embodiment of omniscience; yet the Tathāgata does not engage in volitional thought, for his mind is free from effortful activity.

“Mañjuśrī, it is like a crystal maṇi jewel that has been well polished and refined; wherever it is placed, it serves as an ornament—whether adorning the feet, the hands, the head, or the neck—in every place where it is adorned there is great radiance, and all other ornaments follow along with that light.”

Mañjuśrī! As the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, moves through the four modes of deportment and dwells wherever he may be, wherever the Tathāgata’s radiance shines, there too light shines; yet the Tathāgata does not engage in volitional thought, for his mind is free from effortful application.

“Mañjuśrī! Just as the earth supports all various kinds of grasses, shrubs, medicinal herbs, and trees, causing them all to grow, yet the earth does not engage in volitional thought, deliberation, or discrimination.”

Mañjuśrī! Just as the Tathāgata abides within all sentient beings so that their roots of goodness increase, the Tathāgata does not engage in volitional thought; his mind is without effortful activity.

“Mañjuśrī! It is just as when a great cloud covers the entire earth and sends down rain of a single flavor upon all kinds of things, causing the grasses and trees to take on various flavors and various colors, yet the cloud does not engage in volitional thought or discrimination.”

Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, uses clouds of Buddha-bodies to universally cover the various roots of goodness, various vows, various liberations of mind, and various abidings in liberation of sentient beings, raining down the great Dharma rain so that their various roots of goodness, various vows, and various liberations of mind all attain growth.
The Tathāgata also does not form such a thought or reflection: "I shall cause the roots of goodness of these sentient beings as śrāvakas to increase;
I shall cause the roots of goodness of these sentient beings as pratyekabuddhas to increase; I shall cause the roots of goodness of these sentient beings toward the wisdom of a Buddha to increase;
I shall cause the roots of goodness of these sentient beings for birth among the Four Heavenly Kings to increase."
I cause the roots of goodness for rebirth among the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens to increase in these sentient beings;

I cause the roots of goodness for rebirth among the gods of the Yāma Heaven to increase in these sentient beings; I cause the roots of goodness for rebirth among the gods of the Tuṣita Heaven to increase in these sentient beings;
I cause the roots of goodness for rebirth among the gods of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven to increase in these sentient beings; I cause...
I cause the roots of goodness of these sentient beings born in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations to increase;
I cause the roots of goodness of these sentient beings, up to those born in the Five Pure Abodes, to increase.

Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata does not engage in conceptual discrimination, thinking: "I shall cause this being to increase various roots of goodness born of royalty; I shall cause this being to increase roots of goodness born of the human state; I shall cause this being to increase roots of goodness born of wealth and nobility."

Mañjuśrī! Although the Tathāgata does not engage in intentional conceptualization, his activities for the benefit of others are accomplished according to their vows, their inclinations, and their aspirations; through the maturation of their roots of goodness, he constantly practices equanimity in all places, without thought or conceptualization.
“Mañjuśrī! Just as when the sun first rises, it emits immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of rays of light, dispelling all darkness throughout Jambudvīpa;
yet the light does not form the intention, ‘I shall extinguish the darkness,’ for although it is devoid of thought, its function is accomplished through the day.”

Mañjuśrī! When the Buddha-sun first rises, it emits immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of rays of wisdom-light, extinguishing the darkness of false views; the Tathāgata manifests in response to bring sentient beings to maturity.

Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata likewise does not engage in intentional discrimination, thinking, "I shall extinguish the afflictions and wrong views of sentient beings," for the deeds of a Tathāgata are accomplished without effortful exertion.

“Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, it is like a magician who manifests various things; without effort and without deliberation, the illusory things he creates are accomplished spontaneously. These manifested illusions are ineffable, neither arising nor ceasing, without letters, without sound, without nature, and without marks. They are inconceivable, neither going nor coming, without equal and without counterpart.”

Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, manifests in all places through the four modes of deportment for the sake of all sentient beings; yet this Tathāgata is ineffable, neither arising nor ceasing, without letters and without sound, without nature and without marks, inconceivable, neither going nor coming, peerless and without counterpart, equal to the Dharma-realm.

“Mañjuśrī! Just as the sun, over Mount Sumeru and the four continents, is seen differently by sentient beings—some see the sun rising, some see it setting, some see it at midday, and some see it at midnight—the sun itself does not engage in volitional thought or discrimination; yet, due to Mount Sumeru, various phenomena appear within the world of the four continents, resulting in these differing perceptions.”

Mañjuśrī! In a single assembly, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha causes all sentient beings to have various different perceptions: some see the Tathāgata as one who is about to attain Buddhahood; some see the Tathāgata as one who is about to enter parinirvāṇa; some see the Tathāgata as one who has already attained Buddhahood; some see the Tathāgata as one who has already entered parinirvāṇa; some see the Tathāgata’s True Dharma flourishing; some see the Tathāgata’s True Dharma declining and vanishing; some see the Tathāgata preaching the Dharma for ten, twenty, or up to forty years; and some see the Tathāgata having entered parinirvāṇa ten, twenty, thirty, forty, or even hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of unspeakable kalpas ago.
“Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata likewise does not engage in intentional conceptualization; it is due to sentient beings that he appears differently to each. Mañjuśrī!”

Just as when a great wind blows across Jambudvīpa, the grasses and trees of the east all bow down simultaneously while those of the west all rise up simultaneously; thus, they rise and fall in various ways according to their respective directions, yet these grasses and trees do not engage in volitional thought or reflection, for it is by the blowing of the wind that these various manifestations appear.

Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha manifests the four modes of deportment throughout incalculable eons for the sake of sentient beings. If sentient beings, taking the Tathāgata as their object of focus, give rise to various practices, they will sever rebirth in the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, the animal realm, and the world of King Yama for incalculable eons.

If there are sentient beings who, for even a single thought-moment, direct their attention toward the Tathāgata, the merit they obtain will be limitless and beyond measure; even hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of great bodhisattvas, all of whom have attained inconceivable liberation and meditative concentration, would be unable to calculate or fathom its boundaries.

“Mañjuśrī! It is like the sun rising from the great ocean, emitting countless, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of rays of light; it reveals cities and villages, extinguishes all darkness, dries up mud and mire, causes grasses and trees to grow, and accomplishes myriad tasks, and only then does it move on—the sun does not engage in volitional thought, deliberation, or discrimination.”

Mañjuśrī! The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, having emerged from the ocean of birth and death, abides within the realm of number while emitting immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of rays of wisdom-light, manifesting throughout all worlds in the ten directions. He dispels the darkness of ignorance, dries up the mud of afflictions, causes the roots of goodness to grow, and brings all things to fulfillment; yet he does not move from his original place, nor does the Tathāgata engage in thought or discrimination, and yet everything is accomplished.

“Mañjuśrī! Suppose there were good men or good women who, for as many kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, daily and without ceasing offered food of a hundred flavors and exquisite celestial garments to Buddhas and assemblies of śrāvakas as numerous as the atoms in the worlds of the ten directions.

Furthermore, after those Tathāgatas had all entered parinirvāṇa, they would erect for each and every Buddha as many stūpas as there are atoms in the worlds of the ten directions—stūpas made of Jambūnada gold, with grounds paved with lightning-flash maṇi jewels, bases made of *sarva-prabhāsa-samcaya* maṇi jewels, banners of genuine maṇi jewels, and canopies of *vaśavartin* maṇi jewels covering them above.”

They construct such stupas, with jeweled canopies covering the entire great trichiliocosm; each banner-cloth, each pennant and flower, each sovereign king of incense, each maṇi jewel, and each wish-fulfilling maṇi jewel—numbering as many as clouds—is scattered as an offering. This is done three times every day without fail for a full period of *saṃkhyeya* kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Furthermore, they instruct countless and immeasurable sentient beings to establish various offerings as described above.

“Mañjuśrī! If there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, with faith, understood this inconceivable realm of the Tathāgata’s merit and wisdom—which transcends all verbal expressions—the merit they would obtain would be infinitely superior to that [of the former].”

Mañjuśrī! If there are bodhisattvas who believe these words, they will be able to fulfill immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of pāramitās; they will be able to know the playful abodes of countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of buddhas; they will be able to shatter countless mountains of pride; they will be able to topple countless banners of jealousy; they will be able to dry up countless rivers of craving; they will be able to cross the sea of countless births and deaths; they will be able to sever the cords of countless māras; they will be able to surpass the radiance of all the suns, moons, Śakras, and Brahmā kings; they will be able to proceed from the realm of one Buddha to the realms of all Buddhas; and they will be able to deliver those born in the hells, as animals, as hungry ghosts, or in the realm of King Yama, causing them to meet the Buddhas and dwell together with bodhisattvas.
"Furthermore, they are able to attain the Sea-Seal Samādhi, the Samādhi of Manifesting All Realms Without Transgression,
the Samādhi of Sovereignty over All Dharmas, the Samādhi of Entering All Dharmas, the Samādhi of Adornment through Non-Action,
the Jewel-Birth Samādhi, the Samādhi of Performing Playful Sports, the Lotus-Adornment Samādhi, and the [Samādhi] that Shatters..."
The Samādhi of Space, the Samādhi that Follows All Worlds, the Lotus Sūtra Samādhi,
the Samādhi of Sovereignty over Realms, the Great Yawn Samādhi, the Samādhi of Sovereignty over Mental Activity,
the Lion’s Yawn Samādhi, the Sun-like Samādhi, the Boundless Revolution Samādhi, and the Samādhi that Flows According to Conditions.
Samādhis: the Vajra-object Samādhi, the Vajra-banner Samādhi, the Vajra-like Samādhi, the Vajra Samādhi,
the Earth-holding Samādhi, the Mountain-equal Samādhi, the Meru-banner Samādhi,
the Treasure-treasury Samādhi, the Mind-mastery Samādhi, and the Mind-mastery of all sentient beings.
The samādhi of all conditioned phenomena as the sphere of practice; the samādhi of profound and secret skillful means;
the samādhi of various eloquent expositions; the samādhi of non-contemplation; the samādhi of contemplating all dharmas;
the samādhi of playful sport; the samādhi of universal passage; the samādhi of surpassing the realm of Māra; the samādhi of manifestation...
The samādhi of all forms, the samādhi of cultivating the body, the samādhi that accords with the principles of all dharmas,
the samādhi of the lamp of wisdom, the samādhi of realizing the light of bodhi, the samādhi of expounding the four unimpeded knowledges,
the samādhi of entering the merit of all practices, the samādhi of explaining all distinctions, and the samādhi of tranquility.
He attained the Samādhi of Discerning Supernatural Powers, the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, and the Samādhi of the Great, Profound, and Immeasurable Shore of the Ocean;
he attained such countless hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of samādhis as these.

Furthermore, he attained the *dhāraṇī* of the infinite array of physical forms and attributes of the Buddhas, the *dhāraṇī* of wisdom, the *dhāraṇī* of pure vocal resonance, the *dhāraṇī* of the inexhaustible treasury, the *dhāraṇī* of boundless transformation, the *dhāraṇī* of the ocean-seal, the *dhāraṇī* of lotus adornment, the *dhāraṇī* of the gate of non-attachment, the *dhāraṇī* of transcending analytical discrimination, and the *dhāraṇī* of upholding the adornments of the Buddhas. He attained such *dhāraṇīs* as these, numbering incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *nayutas*. He reached all supreme practices; he reached the state of knowing all phenomena without depending on others; he reached the state of being free from doubt regarding all phenomena. Furthermore, he attained incalculable hundreds of thousands of Buddha-playful manifestations (*buddha-vikrīḍita*), and he further attained the skillful means of all supreme practices.

“Mañjuśrī! Just as Mount Sumeru is preeminent in its radiance among all mountains, so too, for a bodhisattva who has faith in these words, their radiance of all roots of goodness is the most excellent of all.”
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī said to the bodhisattva Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin:
"Son of the Buddha!
Is there yet another superior dharma, a point of faith and delight for a bodhisattva, such that if a bodhisattva can have faith in it, they will obtain immeasurable and supreme merit?"
The Bodhisattva Subduer of All Veils said:
“There are five dharmas that serve as the basis for a bodhisattva’s faith and delight, through which one attains immeasurable and supreme merit.
What are these five dharmas?”
First, they believe that all dharmas are without opposition, neither arising nor ceasing, and ineffable;

second, they believe that the activities and dignified conducts exceeding the number of dust motes in Jambudvīpa arise spontaneously in every thought-moment through the Tathāgata—not by means of merit or deliberation;
third, they believe that he constantly matures sentient beings, having already attained Buddhahood long ago throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Fourth, one has faith that from the time of following Dīpaṃkara Buddha until the attainment of Buddhahood, all that was performed in the interim is the Buddha’s realm; having attained Buddhahood long ago through infinite eons, he manifests these deeds now.
Fifth, one has faith that the extinction of the Śākya clan and the manifestation of these events are the Buddha’s realm for the purpose of maturing sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī! These are called the five dharmas, which are what the bodhisattva has faith in, whereby he attains boundless and supreme merit. Mañjuśrī!

If there are sons or daughters of good family who, day after day, provide food of a hundred flavors and exquisite garments as offerings to Arhats who have attained the six supernormal powers and the eight liberations for a full eon as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
and if there are other sons or daughters of good family who, within a single day, provide the same offerings to a single Pratyekabuddha—the latter’s merit surpasses that obtained by the former.
Mañjuśrī! If there were good sons or good daughters who, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, were to erect stupas and monasteries as numerous as motes of dust,
and in each and every world, [construct them] from genuine Jāmbūnada gold and *vidyutpradīpa* maṇi-jewels...
The ground was spread with jewels, with clusters of all-luminous maṇi-jewels forming its foundation;
pearl maṇi-jewels served as banners and canopies; gośīrṣa sandalwood was used to smear the ground;
sovereign king maṇi-jewels formed a net placed above to cover it; and ocean-pure universal-light-adorned maṇi-jewels served as pillars.
The top was covered with lion-maned *maṇi* jewels, and lion-bannered *maṇi* gems served as windows;

various banners and canopies were suspended there. It was the dwelling place of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of *pratyekabuddhas*, to whom one offered food of a hundred flavors and exquisite garments every day for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Mañjuśrī! If there is a son of good family or a daughter of good family who hears "Buddha," "World-Honored One," "Tathāgata," or "Omniscient One," the merit obtained by this son or daughter of good family surpasses that [of the former] immeasurably and beyond calculation.

Mañjuśrī! If there should be another son or daughter of good family who creates an image of the Buddha—whether by means of painting with colors or using clay or wood—the merit obtained by that person would again surpass the former, being incalculable and immeasurable; how much more so when one offers various kinds of worship such as incense, flowers, banners, and canopies, the merit obtained would be infinite, boundless, and beyond all reckoning.

Furthermore, if there are sons or daughters of good family who take refuge in the Tathāgata and observe the Tathāgata’s prohibitive precepts for a single day, the merit obtained by such persons will surpass that of the former by an immeasurable, incalculable, and unfathomable degree.

“Mañjuśrī! Furthermore, if there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, with food of a hundred flavors and a hundred kinds of exquisite garments, made offerings to all the Buddhas,
as well as the bodhisattvas and the great assembly of śrāvakas throughout the ten directions, for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges River...”
Throughout those kalpas, when those Tathāgatas enter parinirvāṇa, for each and every Tathāgata,
one shall erect jeweled stupas as numerous as the atoms within the worlds of the ten directions; each jeweled stupa shall be as vast in length and breadth as the four continents,
fully adorned and complete, with floors spread with lamps made of true Jambūnada gold and maṇi jewels.
It was founded upon a base of *maṇi* jewels from which all light emanates; pearl *maṇi* jewels formed its banners and canopies;
its ground was anointed with gośīrṣa sandalwood; and it was covered above by a net of *maṇi* jewels known as Sovereign Kings (*vairocana-rāja*).
Furthermore, precious canopies completely covered the trichiliocosm, and there were banners and flowers of such numbers that they could not be counted.
Like clouds, they further offered various kinds of exquisite music and dance as an offering to the stūpa. Mañjuśrī!

If there should be another son or daughter of good family who can believe that the merit and wisdom of the Tathāgata are inconceivable, and even gives a single mouthful of food to an animal, the merit obtained by this person shall again surpass the former, beyond measure.

“Mañjuśrī! If there is a bodhisattva who believes in the sūtras and makes offerings as previously described, and if there is another bodhisattva who believes in this dharma of the sūtra and, seeing others who believe in this dharma, gives rise to great joy and a heart of exultation, conceives a mind of reverence, greets them with joined palms, bows in prostration, and inquires after their well-being, making offerings according to what they are able to provide—the merit of this person shall again surpass that of the former by an immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable amount.”
"Why is this? Because these merits can give rise to the Buddha-wisdom, as sealed by the World-Honored One.

Having heard these words, Mañjuśrī was filled with great joy, as were the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, along with the devas, humans, asuras, garuḍas, and others; they all rejoiced, prostrated themselves, and withdrew.
The Sūtra on the Adornment of the Light of Wisdom that Transcends the Realms of All Buddhas
